To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

monoclonal antibodies directed against epitopes outside of the myogenin bHLH domain bind to epitopes that are masked in heterodimers with E12 and interfere with DNA binding by the myogenin-E12 heterodimer.
monoclonal antibodies to the myogenin protein interfere with the DNA binding of myogenins/E-proteins heterodimers.

monoclonal antimyogenic antibodies recognize epitopes spanning the myogenic molecule outside the bHLHL domain and that some antibodies interfere with the DNA binding of myogenine protein-protein complexes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of monoclonal antibody technology to define the surfaces of myogenin and other bHLH proteins that are important for their interactions with other proteins, and with DNA.
the development of a panel of monoconal antibodies against myogenin and their use in defining the epitopes and their role in the function of the protein.
the use of antibodies to map the structure and function of the myogenic regulatory factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the binding of antibodies to epitopes outside the myogenin HLH domain can interfere with protein-protein or protein-DNA interactions.
the monoclonal antibodies we describe in this paper define epitopes outside of the bHLh domain where binding interfered with protein-protein or protein-DNA interactions.

the epitopes of the monoclonal antibodies described in the present paper are not located in the DNA binding domain and that the epitopes are not located in regions of the myogenin molecule that interact with E-proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the monoclonals we have developed are useful tools for studying myogenin and other bHLH proteins, and that the epitopes they recognize may contribute to the structure and function of these proteins.

monoclonal antibodies directed against epitopes outside of the bHLh domain interfere with the myogenin/DNA interaction and that the epitopes recognized by these antibodies are partially masked in heterodimers.
the myogenin bHLH domain is not the sole determinant of myogenin's DNA binding specificity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
antibodies that bind to epitopes outside the HLH domain can be used to probe the interactions of myogenin with E-proteins and with DNA.
the monoclonal antibody panel we have generated is a useful resource for the characterization of myogenin and its interaction partners.
the binding of monoclonal anti-myogenin antibodies to epitopes outside the HLH domain can interfere with the binding to DNA of myogenin and myogenin/E-Protein complexes.
